opus-5.5.text:
I think the early demonstrations were genuinely exciting, but we have to be honest about what they actually showed. Most of those videos were recorded in very controlled settings: a fixed tabletop, a known set of objects, consistent lighting, and often a lot of trial runs behind the one clip that ended up on social media. So what you saw was the best case, not the typical case.

When you move to real-world deployment, a few problems become obvious very quickly. The first is generalization. A model trained on a few hundred hours of teleoperated data in one lab doesn't automatically transfer to a different kitchen, a different gripper, or even the same room at a different time of day. The vision-language part may understand "pick up the red cup," but the action part is still quite brittle when the scene shifts even a little.

The second is reliability. In a demo, a 70 or 80 percent success rate looks impressive. In a factory or a home, that's basically unusable. People expect something closer to 99-plus percent, and more importantly, they expect the robot to fail gracefully, to know when it's uncertain and to recover rather than knocking things over. Early systems didn't really have that notion of self-correction or long-horizon robustness.

The third is speed and cost. Many of those demos were sped up, or the robot was moving quite slowly to stay safe. Inference latency on large models was also an issue, so you get this gap between how fluid the video looks and what the real control loop can actually sustain.

And underneath all of this is the data problem. Language models had the whole internet; robotics doesn't have an equivalent corpus of action data. So I'd say the early demos proved the direction is promising, that you can connect perception, language, and action in one model, but they didn't yet prove deployability. Closing that gap is really about data scale, better evaluation in messy environments, and building systems that are honest about their own failure modes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yujun Shen: I think the honest answer is that most of those early demos were showing you the best of maybe fifty or a hundred attempts, in a scene that someone had set up very carefully. The lighting is fixed, the objects are placed exactly where the model has seen them during data collection, the table is the same table. And then you take that exact system, move it three meters to the left, change the tablecloth, and it falls apart. So the first limitation is just that the generalization we were implicitly claiming wasn't really there yet.

The second thing is about what the model actually learned. A lot of those demos were essentially memorization of a narrow data distribution dressed up as understanding. The vision-language part gives you this impression of semantic grounding, because the model can parse the instruction "put the red cup on the shelf," but the action head was trained on so little data that the mapping from language to motion was very brittle. You could say "mug" instead of "cup" and the whole thing drifts.

Then there's the long-horizon problem. A pick-and-place in a demo is a few seconds. Real deployment means doing something for minutes or hours, recovering from your own mistakes, noticing that you dropped the object. Early systems had almost no mechanism for recovery, because the training data was mostly clean, successful trajectories. Nobody collected data of the robot failing and then fixing it.

And the last piece, which I think people underestimated, is the physical side. Latency, the gap between the simulator or the data-collection rig and the actual hardware you ship, wear on the gripper, calibration drifting over a week. None of that shows up in a two-minute video.

So I don't want to be too negative, those demos were important, they convinced a lot of people that the direction was worth investing in. But I would say they were existence proofs, not evidence of deployability. The real work since then has been closing exactly those gaps, with much larger and more diverse data, explicit failure recovery, and much more boring engineering on the hardware side.

astra-6.text:
I think the main limitation is the gap between showing that a robot can do something once and showing that it can do it reliably in the real world. An early demonstration may involve a carefully arranged environment, a narrow task, and familiar objects. That’s a useful proof of concept, but it doesn’t tell us how the system behaves when those conditions change.

For deployment, you need to understand the failures as much as the successes. What happens when an object slips, someone interrupts the task, or the robot encounters something unfamiliar? Can it detect the problem, recover, or ask for help? So I would look beyond an impressive demonstration and ask about repeated performance, the amount of human intervention, and the range of conditions tested. That’s where the real deployment challenge becomes clear.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main limitation is the gap between showing that a robot can do something once and showing that it can do it reliably in the real world. An early demonstration might use a carefully arranged environment, a narrow task, and familiar objects. That’s useful for proving an idea, but it doesn’t tell us how the system behaves when the lighting changes, an object moves, or an action fails halfway through.

For deployment, we need to understand the failure rate, how much human intervention is required, and whether the robot can recover safely. So I would treat those early demonstrations as evidence of possibility. The next step is to establish robustness across repeated trials and varied conditions.
